read.sections.1.text.back: Many communities make objects that have cultural meaning. In Ghana, weavers make kente cloth from narrow woven strips sewn together into one. Many kente patterns have names, and some of those names come from proverbs or events in history. In Indonesia, people decorate batik cloth with hot wax and dye. Batik is used throughout life, from cloth for carrying a baby to clothes for weddings. In the Pacific, in places like Tonga and Fiji, people beat tree bark to make tapa cloth. This cloth is often made together by a group of people, and used at weddings and other big events.
read.sections.1.text.source: Many communities make objects with cultural meaning. In Ghana, weavers make kente cloth from narrow strips that are sewn together. Many kente patterns have names, and some names come from proverbs or events in history. In Indonesia, people decorate batik cloth with hot wax and dye. Batik is used through life, from cloths that carry babies to clothes for weddings. In the Pacific, in places such as Tonga and Fiji, people beat tree bark to make tapa cloth. Groups often make it together, and it is used at weddings and other big events.

watch.summary.note: 'Small green pot' from China = 'guci kecil' (ceramic jar), because 'pot' in Indonesian suggests a flower pot. Check it fits the object in the video.
watch.summary.back: This short video comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. The video discusses three everyday objects from that museum. The first is a small green (ceramic) jar from China. In the past, people in the Philippines traded to get jars and bowls from China. Most were plain, but this jar has pictures of two dragons. The second is a salakot, a wide hat woven from plants. Many ordinary people wore it. But some salakot were decorated with shells and silver for important people. The third is a small cloth called a handkerchief. If you look carefully, you can see a sad poem sewn on the cloth. The video says that materials and skill make an object valuable. But the story and context around it make the object even more special.
watch.summary.source: This short video comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. It looks at three everyday objects from the museum. The first is a small green pot from China. Long ago, people in the Philippines traded for Chinese pots and bowls. Most were plain, but this one has two dragons on it. The second is the salakot, a wide hat woven from plants. Many ordinary people wore it. But some salakot were decorated with shell and silver for important people. The third is a small cloth called a handkerchief. If you look closely, you can see a sad poem sewn into it. The video says the materials and the skill make an object valuable. But the stories and context around it make it even more special.

read.sections.0.heading.back: One object can have many meanings
read.sections.0.heading.source: One object can have many meanings

read.sections.0.text.back: Look at the woven bag in the evidence part. The seller says the bag was made for carrying food and books. That is its practical use. The owner says their aunt gave them the bag when they started at a new school, so the bag also holds a memory. Its makers, a craft group, learned the pattern from older weavers. For them, the bag shows a skill. There is only one bag, but each person sees it from a different point of view. To understand an object, you need to know the object's context: who made it, who uses it, and why.

For them, the bag shows a skill. It is one bag, but each person sees it from a different perspective. To understand an object, you need its context: who made it, who uses it, and why.

read.sections.2.text.back: A museum label tells visitors about an object. The first label for the bag only said "Everyday carry bag". That is true, but the label does not mention the memory and the skill. Guessing the meaning of the pattern is also a mistake. A label that calls the pattern a symbol of the whole community, with no source, is a weak label. People in one group do not necessarily see an object the same way. A better label uses evidence from the makers and users. It says what we know and what we still need to ask.
read.sections.2.text.source: A museum label tells visitors about an object. The first label for the bag says only “Everyday carrying bag”. That is true, but it misses the memory and the skill. It is also a mistake to guess what the pattern means. A label that calls the pattern a symbol of a whole community, with no source, is weak. People in one group may not all see an object in the same way. A better label uses evidence from the makers and users. It says what we know and what we still need to ask.

The label also says what we still need to ask.

write.example.back: This bag is used for carrying food and books. For its owner, this bag is also a memory. Their aunt gave them this bag when they started at a new school. For its makers, this pattern shows a skill they learned from older weavers. Before we explain this pattern, we need to ask the craft group what this pattern means to them. This shows that one object can have many meanings. A good label says whose point of view it uses.
